subtype: Approach: batches so long that urgent matters wait too long [Pitfall]
passage: Lars had read that answering messages once a day saves time, so from Monday he opened the team chat only at five o'clock. On Wednesday at ten past nine in the Rotterdam office, Tuan wrote: "The client asks whether the delivery can move to Thursday. They need an answer before noon." Tuan waited, wrote again at eleven, and again at half past twelve. Lars was in meetings and did not look. By noon Tuan had told the client, "I'll get back to you today." The client, who had another supplier ready, went with them. At five Lars read all the messages together and went cold. "Why didn't you call me?" Tuan said, "You said no calls unless it's an emergency, and I didn't know if this counted."

qa.q: At what time did Lars open the team chat?
qa.a: Lars opened the team chat only at five o'clock.

qa.q: How did Lars feel on reading the messages at five?
qa.a: Lars felt shocked and regretful, and went cold.

qa.q: What could Lars do so that urgent questions are seen?
qa.a: Lars could keep the fixed message slots but agree on a call or a flagged word for urgent client matters, and check for it more often.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt while waiting through the morning?
qa.a: Tuan may have felt anxious and stuck, unsure whether to phone, as the client's deadline came closer.

grounding: Shows a manager answering messages only once a day so a colleague's urgent client question sits unanswered until evening.
